\chapter{Where The Town Goes When The Work Stops}
\label{ch:el-hotel-y-el-cine}
\hlchaptermodality{354}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el hotel, el restaurante, el cine, el parque and el jardin, and say which one I am going to.}

Complete ES-C354-jardin: name five places you go when the work is done, and say which one you are going to.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el hotel]{el hotel — the same word as hospital, worn down in France}

\label{lesson:ES-C354-hotel}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the library}, then \emph{the museum}. (\emph{La biblioteca}; \emph{el museo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el hospital — the same Latin word, taken by a different road.
  \item la maleta — what you carry in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o-TEL}, two beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{h} goes unsaid, the same way it did in \emph{el hospital}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el hotel} — \textquotedblleft{}the hotel.\textquotedblright{}

You already have this word. It is \textbf{hospitāle} again, the guest house from the last chapter, arriving by a longer and rougher road.

Old French said \textbf{hostel}. Then French did to that \emph{s} what French does to almost every \emph{s} before a consonant: it dropped it. What is left behind is the little hat — \emph{hôtel} — which is a headstone marking the spot. The same hat stands over \emph{forêt} for \emph{forest}, \emph{île} for \emph{isle}, \emph{pâte} for \emph{paste}.

English borrowed the word twice, once before the \emph{s} fell and once after, so English has both \textbf{hostel} and \textbf{hotel} and treats them as different things.

Spanish had no need of it — it already had \emph{hospital}, and \emph{la posada} and \emph{el mesón} for an inn — so \textbf{hotel} came late, straight from French, with its foreign stress on the last beat still attached.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A place to sleep, and a rule of thumb for reading French words with a hat on them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el hotel}
  \item \emph{un hotel}
  \item \emph{¿dónde está el hotel?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter does the French circumflex stand in for? (A lost \emph{s}.) And which Spanish word is \emph{hotel} a cousin of? (\emph{Hospital}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el restaurante]{el restaurante — a soup that turned into a room}

\label{lesson:ES-C354-restaurante}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the museum}, then \emph{the hotel}. (\emph{El museo}; \emph{el hotel}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la comida — what it sells.
  \item el plato — what it arrives on.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{res-tau-RAN-te}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{au} is one glide, not two beats. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el restaurante} — \textquotedblleft{}the restaurant.\textquotedblright{}

In Paris in the 1760s, a \textbf{restaurant} was something you drank. It was a strong meat broth, sold to people who felt weak — a \emph{restorative}. The word is the French present participle of \textbf{restaurer}: a thing that restores.

Shops opened to sell it. They were called \emph{restaurants} after the broth, the way a chocolate shop is named after chocolate. Then the shops started serving other food, and other food at small tables, and within thirty years the word had climbed off the soup and onto the room.

Latin \textbf{restaurāre} is \emph{re-} plus \textbf{instaurāre}, to set up — so to restore is to set a thing up again. English took it whole as \textbf{restore} and Spanish as \emph{restaurar}, and both still mean putting a thing back the way it was.

Which is a fair description of what a good meal does.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The place to eat when the food is not at home.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el restaurante}
  \item \emph{un restaurante}
  \item \emph{comer en el restaurante}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{restaurant} before it was a room? (A restorative broth.) And what does \emph{restaurar} mean? (To put a thing back as it was.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el cine]{el cine — a movement-writer, cut down to one syllable}

\label{lesson:ES-C354-cine}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the hotel}, then \emph{the restaurant}. (\emph{El hotel}; \emph{el restaurante}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ver — what you do there.
  \item la luz — what they turn off first.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SI-ne}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} before \emph{e} is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el cine} — \textquotedblleft{}the cinema,\textquotedblright{} and the art as well as the building.

The Lumière brothers needed a name for their machine and did what the nineteenth century always did: they went to Greek. \textbf{Kínēma} is a movement, from \textbf{kineîn}, to move. \textbf{Gráphein} is to write or scratch. Bolt them together and you have a \emph{cinématographe}, a movement-writer.

Nobody was going to say that twice. Spanish sheared off everything after the first two beats and kept \textbf{el cine}. English kept a different piece and got \textbf{cinema}. German kept a third and got \emph{Kino}. Three languages, one word, cut in three places.

\textbf{Kineîn} survives uncut in English \textbf{kinetic}, and in \emph{kinesiology} and \emph{telekinesis}.

And \textbf{gráphein} you have met already, in the \emph{-graphy} of bibliography — the book-writing that lives next door to \emph{la biblioteca}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word that is a stump of a much longer one, and the Greek verb for moving.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cine}
  \item \emph{un cine}
  \item \emph{vamos al cine}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{kínēma} mean? (Movement.) And what was the full word Spanish cut \emph{cine} out of? (\emph{Cinematógrafo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el parque]{el parque — the fence, not the grass}

\label{lesson:ES-C354-parque}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the restaurant}, then \emph{the cinema}. (\emph{El restaurante}; \emph{el cine}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el árbol — what stands in it.
  \item el banco — the word you now own twice.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PAR-ke}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{qu} is a plain hard \emph{k}; the \emph{u} is silent. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el parque} — \textquotedblleft{}the park.\textquotedblright{}

The oldest meaning of this word is a fence.

Frankish \textbf{parrik} was an enclosure, and Medieval Latin wrote it \textbf{parricus}. A \emph{park} was a piece of ground a lord had fenced so that the deer inside it stayed inside it and the villagers outside it stayed outside. Nothing in the word is about grass, or trees, or benches. It is about the boundary.

English has the same word twice: \textbf{park}, and the dialect \textbf{paddock}, which is \emph{parrock} with the \emph{r} and the \emph{d} swapped around the way spoken words do.

What changed is who the fence is for. A royal park kept people out. A city park, which is a nineteenth-century idea, keeps a piece of green from being built on — the fence now protects the grass from the town rather than the deer from the villagers.

And when the motor car arrived, Spanish put it in the enclosure too, and got \emph{aparcar}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A green square with a fence in its history, and the seat you already know how to name.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el parque}
  \item \emph{un parque}
  \item \emph{el banco está en el parque}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a park before it was grass? (A fenced enclosure.) And what was kept inside the fence? (Deer.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el jardín]{el jardín — the second fence in a row}

\label{lesson:ES-C354-jardin}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the cinema}, then \emph{the park}. (\emph{El cine}; \emph{el parque}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la flor — what grows in it.
  \item el parque — the other enclosure.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{jar-DIN}, two beats with the weight on the last, which is why it carries a written accent. The \emph{j} is the rough Spanish sound at the back. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el jardín} — \textquotedblleft{}the garden.\textquotedblright{}

Two fences in a row. \emph{El parque} came from a Frankish enclosure, and so does this one: \textbf{gardo}, a Germanic word for a fenced piece of ground, which French took as \emph{jardin} and Spanish took from French.

English has the same word without the French detour. A \textbf{yard} is \emph{gardo} arriving on its own, straight down the Germanic road. Then English borrowed the French shape back on top, and now it has \textbf{yard} and \textbf{garden} side by side and treats them as different sizes of the same thing.

The enclosure shows up in places English does not think of as words about fences:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{kindergarten}, a children's enclosure, named by the German who invented it because he thought children should be grown rather than taught;
  \item \textbf{Stuttgart}, a stud-farm enclosure;
  \item \textbf{Asgard}, the enclosure of the Norse gods;
  \item and the \emph{-chard} of \textbf{orchard}, which is a wort-yard, a herb enclosure.
\end{itemize}

So a garden, a farmyard and the home of Odin are one Germanic fence.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five places to go when the work is done: \emph{el hotel}, \emph{el restaurante}, \emph{el cine}, \emph{el parque}, \emph{el jardín}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el jardín}
  \item \emph{el hotel, el restaurante, el cine, el parque}
  \item \emph{¿dónde está el jardín?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which plain English word is the same Germanic word as \emph{jardín}? (Yard.) And what is a kindergarten, word for word? (A children's garden.)
\end{tcolorbox}
